<!-- theorema-1: body_md -->
For every $n\geq4$, as convergent logarithmic germs at $s=-\infty$,
\[
 I^{(n-1)}_\circleddash(s)=(-1)^{n-1}yA\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k\gamma_k\,
 \mathcal T_{n-1-k}(R,Q),
\]
where $\theta_Q=Q\,d/dQ$ and
\[
 \mathcal T_j=\frac{n!}{j!}R^j
 -\sum_{a=0}^{j-2}\frac{(n-2-a)!}{(j-a-2)!}R^{j-a-2}\mathcal D_a^\Delta
 -\sum_{a=0}^{j-1}\frac{(n-2-a)!}{(j-a-1)!}R^{j-a-1}\theta_Q\mathcal D_a^\Delta .
\]
In particular,
\[
 I^{(n-1)}_\circleddash(s)=(-1)^{n-1}yA\Bigl[nR^{n-1}
 -\theta_Q\mathcal D_0^\Delta\,R^{n-2}
 -\bigl((n-2)\mathcal D_0^\Delta+\theta_Q\mathcal D_1^\Delta\bigr)R^{n-3}+\cdots\Bigr],
\]
where the omitted terms have degree at most $n-4$ in $R$; the odd zeta values
first enter there, through the term $-\gamma_3\mathcal T_{n-4}$.
<!-- end theorema-1 -->
<!-- theoremb-1: body_md -->
The mirror map $y\mapsto Q=e^{R(y)}=y+O(y^2)$ is invertible near $y=0$, and
for $0\leq a\leq n-2$,
\[
 \mathcal D_a^\Delta(Q)=-\frac{n!}{(n-2-a)!}\,K_{a+2}\bigl(y(Q)\bigr).
\]
<!-- end theoremb-1 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
A superscript on $H$ carrying a space as argument, as in $H^k(F_n,\mathbb Q)$,
denotes a cohomology group; a bare power $H^k$ denotes the $k$-fold cup
product of the divisor class $H$. The letters $E_\pm$ always denote the
index bundles of Lemma~\ref{lem:basechange} on a stable-map stack,
while $\rho_\pm=\pm H$ and $\mathcal B_\pm=\mathcal O_{Y_n}(\pm H)$ denote
the corresponding cohomology class and line bundle on $Y_n$. The
operators $T_k$ of Definition~\ref{def:operator} carry a subscript and
are unrelated to the tangent bundles $T_{F_n},T_{Y_n},T_{X_n}$, to the assembly
polynomials $\mathcal T_j$ of~\eqref{eq:Vj}, or to the positive
variable $T=-s$ of Section~\ref{sec:analytic}. Similarly $P_{n-1}$ is the
differential operator and $\bar p$ is a sum of passive divisor classes.
Where an external theorem is quoted in full, it is stated at the point of
use, in the notation of its source where this causes no conflict, and the
paragraph following it fixes the translation.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:geometry}
One has
\[
 K_{F_n}=\mathcal O_{F_n}(-H),\quad K_{X_n}\cong\mathcal O_{X_n},\quad
 \int_FH^{n-1}=n!,\quad H_2(F_n,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^n.
\]
Under the last isomorphism $\beta$ corresponds to
$(p_1\cdot\beta,\ldots,p_n\cdot\beta)$. Every effective class has nonnegative
coordinates. In particular, at most $\binom{m+n-1}{n-1}$ effective classes
have $H$-degree $m$. Moreover
\[
 \delta_a=\frac{H^{n-2-a}}{(n-2-a)!}
 =\sum_{|S|=n-2-a}\prod_{i\in S}p_i\in H^{2(n-2-a)}(F_n,\mathbb Z),
 \qquad 0\leq a\leq n-2.
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Adjunction gives $K_{F_n}=(-2H+H)|_{F_n}=-H$.
For a line bundle $E$ on a smooth base, the vertical tangent bundle on
$\operatorname{Tot}(E)$ is the pullback of $E$, so
$K_{\operatorname{Tot}(E)}=\varpi^*(K_{F_n}\otimes E^{-1})$; take $E=K_{F_n}$.
Also $i_*[F_n]=H$, and $H^n=n!p_1\cdots p_n$ on $Y_n$.
The Segre embedding realizes $\mathcal O_{Y_n}(H)$ as a hyperplane bundle.
Apply the integral homology statement of \cite[Corollary~7.3]{Milnor}
to this smooth projective
$n$-fold and its smooth hyperplane section. Since $2<n-1$, it gives
$H_2(F_n,\mathbb Z)=H_2(Y_n,\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^n$. The same theorem in degree zero
makes $F_n$ connected. Since it is smooth, it is irreducible and reduced. Each $p_i$ is nef and $H$ is ample; hence effective
nonzero classes have nonnegative coordinates with positive sum. Counting
all nonnegative tuples gives the stated upper bound, without assuming
that every tuple is represented by an irreducible rational curve.
Finally, expand $H^r$ using $p_i^2=0$, then each square-free monomial occurs
$r!$ times.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:ambient}
The ordinary Poincar\'e pairing on $V_\mathrm{amb}$ is nondegenerate, and
\[
 \ker i^*=\ker(H\cup-:\mathcal R\to\mathcal R),\qquad
 \mathcal R^{S_n}=\mathbb Q[H]/(H^{n+1}).
\]
The radical of $\int_YabH/(\lambda-H)$ over $\mathbb Q(\lambda)$ is also
$\ker i^*$. If $n$ is even, all even cohomology of $F_n$ is ambient.
If $n$ is odd, the only possible nonambient even group is $H^{n-1}(F_n,\mathbb Q)$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
\cite[Corollary~7.3]{Milnor}, followed by \cite[Theorem~3.2]{Hatcher}
over $\mathbb Q$, identifies
cohomology below degree $n-1$ and is injective in degree $n-1$.
Poincar\'e duality applies to the closed oriented real $(2n-2)$-manifold
$F_n(\mathbb C)$ \cite[Theorem~3.30]{Hatcher}. For a degree $k>n-1$, the pairing of
$i^*H^k(Y_n)$ with
$H^{2n-2-k}(F_n)=i^*H^{2n-2-k}(Y_n)$ is represented on $Y_n$ by multiplication
by $H$. Lemma~\ref{lem:linearlefschetz} below says this multiplication has the required
full rank, so $i^*$ is surjective in degree $k$. In degree $n-1$ the
bilinear form $\int_YabH$ on $H^{n-1}(Y_n)$ is nondegenerate because
$H:H^{n-1}(Y_n)\to H^{n+1}(Y_n)$ is an isomorphism by that lemma ($\dim_\mathbb C Y_n=n$).
These facts prove nondegeneracy on the ambient image.
Since $i_*i^*a=Ha$, one inclusion of kernels is immediate; for the other,
if $Ha=0$, then $i^*a$ pairs to zero with every ambient class and is
therefore zero. Multiplication by $(\lambda-H)^{-1}$ is an automorphism
of the ambient algebra, so does not change the radical.
A square-free monomial basis of $\mathcal R$ is indexed by subsets of
$\{1,\ldots,n\}$. An invariant element has constant coefficients on
subsets of each fixed size, whose sum is $H^j/j!$. This proves the
invariant-ring assertion. Finally the only cohomology possibly not
inherited from $Y_n$ is the middle group, by the preceding Lefschetz and
duality arguments.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:linearlefschetz}
In $\mathcal R$, multiplication by $H$ from square-free degree $r$ to
degree $r+1$ is injective for $2r<n$ and surjective for $2r\geq n-1$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Give the monomial basis $p_S$ the orthonormal positive-definite inner
product over $\mathbb R$. Let $U$ multiply by $H$ and put
$Dp_S=\sum_{i\in S}p_{S\setminus\{i\}}$. Then $D=U^*$ and direct
expansion gives $DU-UD=(n-2r)\operatorname{id}$ in degree $r$.
If $Uv=0$ and $2r<n$, then
$0=\|Dv\|^2+(n-2r)\|v\|^2$, so $v=0$.
The complement involution $p_S\mapsto p_{S^c}$ interchanges $U$ and
$D$. Injectivity in complementary degree therefore gives surjectivity
in the stated range. All maps are rational, so the rank conclusions
hold over $\mathbb Q$. In particular the middle map is an isomorphism
when its two graded pieces have the same dimension.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:primitive}
For $n=5$, $\chi(F_n)=40$, $b_2=b_6=5$, and $b_4=28$, whereas the ambient
part of $H^4(F_n,\mathbb Q)$ has dimension $\binom52=10$. Thus the nonambient middle summand
has dimension $18$. These numbers follow from
\[
 \chi(F_n)=n!\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{(-1)^{n-1-k}2^k}{k!},
\]
obtained by integrating the degree-$(n-1)$ part of
$c(TF)=\prod_{i=1}^5(1+2p_i)/(1+H)$; the remaining Betti numbers are forced by
Lefschetz and Poincar\'e duality.
The full Lefschetz-primitive middle group has dimension $28-5=23$;
it includes ambient primitive classes and is distinct from the
$18$-dimensional orthogonal nonambient summand.
This $18$-dimensional summand is the reason the ambientness statement of
Theorem~\ref{thm:fullambient} is needed when $n$ is odd. The four solutions
of the differential operator $P_4$ given in eq.~\eqref{e:P4} correspond to the ambient classes $1,H,H^2,H^3$, and nothing in the
operator sees the orthogonal complement.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:HV}
The root lattice $A_4$ enters this story, but on the mirror side rather than
here. The superpotential of~\eqref{eq:phidef} is
$\phi(x)=n+\sum_{i\ne j}x_ix_j^{-1}$, so its Newton polytope is the convex
hull of the roots $e_i-e_j$, that is the reflexive polytope $\Delta_{A_{n-1}}$.
At $n=5$ the toric closures of the fibers $\{\phi=s\}$, with the small
resolutions described below and at nonsingular parameters, give the Calabi--Yau threefolds of
Hulek--Verrill~\cite{HV}, whose equation
$(\sum_{i=1}^5X_i)(\sum_{i=1}^5a_i/X_i)=a_6$ is the equal-mass member $a_i=1$, $a_6=s$
of their five-parameter family. By eq.~\eqref{eq:LGrelation} this is the
graph hypersurface of the four-loop sunset at momentum $s$.

The Fano fourfold $F_n$ corresponds to the Landau--Ginzburg model
$( (\mathbb C^*)^5/\mathbb C^*,\phi)$, whereas a compactified fiber has dimension three.
The Calabi--Yau counterpart of the latter is an anticanonical hypersurface
in $F_n$, equivalently a complete intersection of two $(1,\ldots,1)$
hypersurfaces in $(\mathbb P^1)^5$; see \cite[Remarks 3 and 9]{Iritani}.
The numbers $h^{11}=26$, $h^{21}=16$ of~\cite[Proposition 3.1]{HV}
belong to the general smooth member of the full twenty-parameter family,
not to the sunset subfamily. For a general member of the five-parameter
family, small resolution of its thirty nodes gives $h^{11}=45$, $h^{12}=5$.
These smooth-family statements must be restricted to nonsingular parameters;
in particular they do not apply without qualification at $s=0,1,9,25$.
The period-generated subvariation is the one generated by the holomorphic
residue form and its Gauss--Manin derivatives. Under the natural coordinate
permutation action this form transforms by the sign character. The
logarithmic volume form on $(\mathbb C^*)^n/\mathbb C^*$ transforms by the determinant
of the standard permutation quotient, namely $\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$,
and $\phi$ is invariant. Thus this is not literally the invariant
subvariation unless the action has first been twisted by the sign character.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:tree}
Let $C$ be a connected nodal curve of arithmetic genus zero and
$f:C\to F_n$ or $f:C\to Y_n$ a nonconstant map of total $H$-degree $m$.
Then
\[
 H^0(C,f^*\mathcal O(-H))=0,\quad
 h^1(C,f^*\mathcal O(-H))=m-1,\quad
 H^1(C,f^*\mathcal O(H))=0.
\]
The last line bundle is globally generated on $C$ and has $h^0=m+1$.
Its evaluation at any smooth marked point is surjective.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Every irreducible component is $\mathbb P^1$ and the dual graph is a tree.
For the negative bundle a section vanishes on each noncontracted
component. On a contracted component it is constant, so matching values
at nodes and connectedness propagate vanishing to all components.
For the positive bundle all component degrees are nonnegative.
Inductively remove a leaf. Sections on the remaining tree and the leaf
can be matched at their common node since evaluation on the leaf is
surjective. The normalization exact sequence then gives $H^1=0$;
the same argument, with a prescribed value at a chosen point, gives
global generation. Riemann--Roch on a genus-zero nodal curve gives
$\chi(M)=\deg M+1$, which proves both ranks.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:artinian}
Let $A$ be a local Artinian $\mathbb C$-algebra with residue field $\mathbb C$,
$C_A\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ a flat proper family, and
$\mathcal L$ an invertible sheaf with $H^0(C_0,\mathcal L_0)=0$.
For every finite $A$-module $J$,
$H^0(C_A,\mathcal L\otimes_A J)=0$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Choose a composition series for $J$ with successive quotients $\mathbb C$.
Flatness of $\mathcal L$ over $A$ makes the induced sequences of sheaves
exact, and their successive quotients are the pushforward of
$\mathcal L_0$ from the closed fiber. Left exactness of $H^0$ proves
vanishing by induction. Lemma~\ref{lem:tree} supplies the hypothesis
for the negative target line bundle. For a square-zero extension
$A'\twoheadrightarrow A$, the difference of two lifted fiber coordinates
lies in this group with $J=\ker(A'\to A)$, so it is zero.
Normalization is needed only on the closed fiber. A smoothing such as
$xy=\epsilon$ over $\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ has no section reducing
to the node and need not admit a componentwise normalization over its base;
the argument applies to it without such an assumption.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:basechange}
For a flat proper finitely presented family $\pi:C\to S$ of such curves
over an arbitrary $\mathbb C$-scheme, with a map $f$ whose fibers have fixed
positive degree $m$, the complexes associated to $M_\pm=f^*\mathcal O(\pm H)$ satisfy
\[
 R\pi_*M_-\simeq E_-[-1],\qquad R\pi_*M_+\simeq E_+,
\]
where $E_-,E_+$ are locally free of ranks $m-1,m+1$ and commute with
arbitrary base change. For a marked section there is an exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow E'_+\longrightarrow E_+
 \longrightarrow\operatorname{ev}^*\mathcal O(H)\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad\operatorname{rk} E'_+=m.
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Cohomology and base change for a perfect object and a finitely presented
flat proper-support complex, in \cite[Tag~0A1H]{Stacks}, applies with
$E=M_\pm$ and $\mathcal G^\bullet=\mathcal O_C$.
Thus $R\pi_*M_\pm$ is perfect and commutes with arbitrary base change.
Its fibers have amplitude $[0,1]$, so locally it can be represented by a
two-term complex of finite locally free modules $N^0\to N^1$.
For $M_-$ the fiber maps are injective by Lemma~\ref{lem:tree}; an
invertible maximal minor makes the map locally split injective. Its
cokernel is locally free. For $M_+$ the fiber maps are surjective and
are locally split surjective, giving a locally free kernel instead.
This proves the derived assertions, including on nonreduced bases.
The marked evaluation map is fiberwise surjective, hence locally split
surjective, and its kernel has the indicated rank. The argument applies
on atlases of the stable-map stacks and descends canonically.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:factorization}
For every $\beta\ne0$ and every number $\ell\geq0$ of markings,
\[
 \overline{\mathcal M}_{0,\ell}(F_n,\beta)
 \xrightarrow{\sim}\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,\ell}(X_n,\beta)
\]
is an isomorphism of stacks, compatible with arbitrary base change.
In particular the local stable-map stack is proper and Deligne--Mumford.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
A map $g:C\to\operatorname{Tot}(K_{F_n})$ over a base $S$ consists of $f=\varpi g:C\to F_n$
and a section of $f^*K_{F_n}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:basechange},
$\pi_*f^*K_{F_n}=0$, so this section is zero over $S$.
Conversely composing a map to $F_n$ with $\iota$ gives a
map to $X_n$. These constructions are inverse and functorial. They preserve
stability because exactly the same components are contracted; automorphism
groups agree because $\iota$ is a monomorphism. Properness and the
Deligne--Mumford property now follow from
\cite[Theorem 3.14]{BM}, $F_n$ is a
smooth projective variety over the characteristic-zero field $\mathbb C$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:virtual}
On the stack in Theorem~\ref{thm:factorization}, put
$\mathcal V=R^1\pi_*f^*K_{F_n}$, of rank $m-1$. Then
\[
 [\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,\ell}(X_n,\beta)]^{\mathrm{vir}}
 =c_{m-1}(\mathcal V)\cap
 [\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,\ell}(F_n,\beta)]^{\mathrm{vir}}.
\]
With the fiber scaling action, the equivariant formula replaces
$c_{m-1}$ by $e_\lambda(\mathcal V)$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Along the zero section the differential of $\varpi$ and of $\iota$ give
the canonical split tangent sequence
$\iota^*T_{X_n}=T_{F_n}\oplus K_{F_n}$. Relative to the smooth Artin stack of
prestable marked curves, the stable-map obstruction complex is therefore
\[
 E_{X_n}=E_{F_n}\oplus\mathcal V^\vee[1],\qquad
 E_{F_n}=(R\pi_*f^*T_{F_n})^\vee.
\]
The assertion includes the morphism of obstruction theories. The projection and
zero section give $d\varpi\circ d\iota=1$, so the splitting of tangent bundles
induces a splitting after derived pushforward and duality, compatible with the
tangential stable-map obstruction morphism. For the normal component, construct
that morphism by the relative differential of the universal evaluation map and
the trace map for the universal curve. In a local trivialization of $K_{F_n}$,
its fiber coordinate pulls back to the zero section of $\mathcal O_{\mathcal C}$
over the entire base, by Theorem~\ref{thm:factorization}. Its differential in
base directions is therefore zero as a morphism of complexes. A change of
trivialization multiplies this coordinate by a unit and adds to its differential
a term proportional to the coordinate, also zero. Hence the normal component is
globally the zero morphism, including over nonreduced bases. Thus the resulting
obstruction theory is $(\phi_{F_n},0):E_{F_n}\oplus\mathcal V^\vee[1]\to\mathbb
L$, with the specified morphism, not just a splitting of its underlying
$K$-class. The intrinsic normal cone is embedded in the vector-bundle stack for
$E_{F_n}$ with zero component in $\mathcal V$. Factoring the zero-section Gysin
map for the enlarged obstruction bundle stack through that of $\mathcal V$ gives
the top Chern class. On a zero-locus chart $Z\subset U$ over an atlas $S$ of the
prestable-curve stack, the relative cone maps are explicitly
\[
 [C_{Z/U}/T_{U/S}|_Z]\hookrightarrow[E_+|_Z/T_{U/S}|_Z]
 \hookrightarrow[E_+|_Z/T_{U/S}|_Z]\oplus\mathcal V,
\]
where the second map has zero $\mathcal V$ coordinate. These are
compatible with descent. Only one zero-section self-intersection in
$\mathcal V$ occurs, producing $c_{m-1}(\mathcal V)$.
For precision, the cone and zero-section construction is that of
\cite[Sections 5 and 7, Proposition 5.3]{BF}. For a zero locus of a
vector-bundle section on a smooth ambient stack, the normal cone maps into
the restricted bundle and the ambient pushforward of the virtual class is
the top Chern class of that bundle, with no regularity of the section or
reducedness of its zero locus required.
The argument just given proves the required split excess formula from
that construction, rather than postulating a comparison from a $K$-class.
It works equivariantly by applying the same construction on finite-dimensional
approximations to the classifying space of the fiber-scaling torus.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:localKexcess}
On the common stack of Theorem~\ref{thm:factorization}, the same split
obstruction morphism gives
\[
 \mathcal O^{\mathrm{vir}}_{X_n}
 =\lambda_{-1}(\mathcal V^\vee)\otimes\mathcal O^{\mathrm{vir}}_{F_n},
 \qquad
 \lambda_{-1}(\mathcal V^\vee)
 =\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}(-1)^j[\Lambda^j\mathcal V^\vee].
\]
Indeed the extra cone coordinate is zero in $\mathcal V$; the Koszul
resolution for its zero section gives the displayed factor in the
alternating Tor construction of the virtual structure sheaf
\cite[Section 2.3, Proposition 1]{Lee}. The subscripts indicate the standard stable-map
obstruction theories for the two targets, not different underlying stacks.
Thus neither virtual classes nor virtual structure sheaves for $F_n$ and
$X_n$ are identified merely from their stack isomorphism.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:virtualcompare}
For every $a\geq0$,
\begin{align}
 j_*\left(e_\lambda(E_-|_{M_{F_n}})[M_{F_n}]^\mathrm{vir}\right)
 &=e(E_+)e_\lambda(E_-)[M_{Y_n}]^\mathrm{vir},\label{eq:pushvirtual}\\
 i_*C_{a,\beta}^\lambda&=H \mathsf E_{a,\beta}^{0,\lambda},\label{eq:pushC}
\end{align}
where
\[
 \mathsf E_{a,\beta}^{\mu,\lambda}
 =(\operatorname{ev}_{Y_n})_*\left(\psi^a e_\mu(E'_+)e_\lambda(E_-)[M_{Y_n}]^\mathrm{vir}\right).
\]
In particular, for every $b\in H^*(Y_n)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ambientpair}
 \int_{F_n} i^*b\,C_{a,\beta}^\lambda
 =\int_Fi^*b\,i^*\mathsf E_{a,\beta}^{0,\lambda}.
\end{equation}

The first identity is also valid with $M_{F_n},M_{Y_n}$ replaced by the corresponding
stacks with any number $\ell\geq0$ of markings, and with the bundles formed
on those stacks. It remains valid after multiplication by products of
cotangent-line classes and evaluation pullbacks. The evaluation identities~\eqref{eq:pushC}--\eqref{eq:ambientpair} use the one-marked notation above.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We prove the virtual comparison with an arbitrary number $\ell\geq0$ of
markings and then take $\ell=1$ for the evaluation formulas. Write
$M_V^{(\ell)}=\overline{\mathcal M}_{0,\ell}(V,\beta_V)$, where
$\beta_{F_n}=\beta$ and $\beta_{Y_n}=i_*\beta$, and put $m=H\cdot\beta>0$. The letter $V$ is a placeholder for either target and is unrelated to the ambient subspace $V_\mathrm{amb}$.
All Chow groups in the argument have rational coefficients. The equivariant
identities are identities with an indeterminate $\lambda$; no limit of an
equivariant pairing is involved.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{1. Universal bundles and the zero stack.}
On $M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}$, let $\pi_{Y_n}:\mathcal C_{Y_n}\to M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}$ and
$f_{Y_n}:\mathcal C_{Y_n}\to Y_n$ be the universal family. By
Lemmas~\ref{lem:tree}--\ref{lem:basechange},
\begin{align*}
 R\pi_{Y_n*}f_{Y_n}^*\mathcal O_{Y_n}(H)&=E_+,
 \qquad R\pi_{Y_n*}f_{Y_n}^*\mathcal O_{Y_n}(-H)=E_-[-1],
 \cr \operatorname{rk}E_+&=m+1,\quad \operatorname{rk}E_-=m-1.
\end{align*}
These are identifications of perfect complexes with arbitrary derived
base change. In applying \cite[Tag~0A1H]{Stacks} on an atlas, the morphism
is the proper flat finitely presented curve family, the perfect object is
the indicated line bundle, and the flat finitely presented complex with
proper support is $\mathcal O_{\mathcal C_{Y_n}}$ in degree zero. Thus the
statement applies to nonreduced and non-Noetherian base changes as well.

Let $s\in H^0(Y_n,\mathcal O_{Y_n}(H))$ define $F_n$. Adjunction gives a section
$\sigma=\pi_{Y_n*}f_{Y_n}^*s$ of $E_+$. For any scheme $S\to M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}$,
the pullback of $\sigma$ is zero if and only if
$f_S^*s=0$ as a section on $\mathcal C_S$. This is precisely the condition
that $f_S$ factor through the closed subscheme $F_n$ of $Y_n$. The factorization
is unique and is compatible with isomorphisms and base change. Composition
with $i$ contracts exactly the same components, so it preserves stability
and the automorphism group. The class on $F_n$ is uniquely determined by its
pushforward, by Proposition~\ref{prop:geometry}. Consequently
$j:M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}\hookrightarrow M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}$ is the zero stack of $\sigma$,
as a closed immersion of stacks.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{2. The relative obstruction-theory morphisms.}
Let $\mathfrak B=\mathfrak M_{0,\ell}$ be the smooth Artin stack of connected
prestable marked genus-zero curves. 
One can replace it with a finite-type open substack containing 
the images of the two stable-map stacks, since these images are quasi-compact.
Its dimension is $\ell-3$.
For $V=F_n,Y_n$, the usual relative stable-map obstruction theory is
\[
 \phi_V:\mathbb E_V=(R\pi_{V*}f_V^*T_V)^\vee
       \longrightarrow\mathbb L_{M_V^{(\ell)}/\mathfrak B}.
\]
The relative stable-map obstruction morphism is the construction following
Proposition 4 of~\cite{BehrendGW}; Propositions 2, 4, and 5 give the
prestable base, the stable-map description, and global resolutions,
respectively. We construct its compatibility here.
Here no stabilization of the source is necessary after composition with
$i$. Hence the universal curve over $M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}$ is the actual pullback
of $\mathcal C_{Y_n}$, and derived base change identifies the corresponding
terms in the obstruction theories.

At this point we use the special convexity of the ambient target. Indeed,
$T_{Y_n}=\bigoplus_{r=1}^n\operatorname{pr}_r^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(2)$, and each
summand has nonnegative degree on every component of every genus-zero
source. Hence the normalization-sequence argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:tree}
gives $H^1(C,f^*T_{Y_n})=0$. It follows that
$M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}\to\mathfrak B$ is smooth, with relative tangent bundle
$\pi_{Y_n*}f_{Y_n}^*T_{Y_n}$, and
$\mathbb E_{Y_n}=(\pi_{Y_n*}f_{Y_n}^*T_{Y_n})^\vee=\Omega_{M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}/\mathfrak B}$.
This convexity statement concerns the ambient target only and does not
assert smoothness of $M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}$.

The normal sequence of the smooth hypersurface,
\[
 0\longrightarrow T_{F_n}\longrightarrow i^*T_{Y_n}
   \xrightarrow{\,ds\,}\mathcal O_{F_n}(H)\longrightarrow0,
\]
gives, after pullback to the universal curve, derived pushforward and
duality, the distinguished triangle
\[
 j^*\mathbb E_{Y_n}\longrightarrow\mathbb E_{F_n}
 \longrightarrow(j^*E_+)^\vee[1]\longrightarrow j^*\mathbb E_{Y_n}[1].
\]
We specify its compatibility with the cotangent triangle. On the zero
stack, the derivative of the universal section in a relative tangent
direction $v\in\pi_*f^*T_{Y_n}$ is $\pi_*(ds(v))$.
Indeed over a square-zero extension, locally writing a lift as
$f+\epsilon v$, the section is
$s(f+\epsilon v)=s(f)+\epsilon ds(v)$; changes of trivialization of
$\mathcal O(H)$ contribute a term proportional to $s(f)$, which vanishes
on $M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}$. Thus this differential is globally well defined and
is exactly the map obtained from the normal sequence.

More explicitly, after a smooth base change from an atlas of $\mathfrak B$
and an étale chart on the resulting smooth ambient algebraic space,
trivialize $E_+$ and write $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{m+1})$.
For the ideal $I=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_{m+1})$, the zero-locus
obstruction theory is the morphism
\[
 [\,(j^*E_+)^\vee\xrightarrow{\,d\sigma\,}
                  j^*\Omega_{M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}/\mathfrak B}\,]
 \longrightarrow \mathbb L_{M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}/\mathfrak B}.
\]
The explicit two-term target on this chart is
\[
 [I/I^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{U/S}|_Z]
       \simeq\tau_{\ge-1}\mathbb L_{Z/S},
\]
where $U\to S$ is the smooth chart just described and $Z=Z(\sigma)$.
It is the truncation, not an identification with the full cotangent
complex unless further lci hypotheses hold. The canonical morphism to
$\mathbb L_{Z/S}$ is supplied by the derived Koszul zero locus; the
following component description is its truncation.
Its degree $-1$ map sends the dual basis to the classes of $\sigma_a$ in
$I/I^2$; its degree zero map is the restriction of relative differentials.
It is an obstruction theory without a regular-sequence hypothesis on
the $\sigma_a$. 
The preceding computation of $d\sigma$ identifies this two-term complex with
$(R\pi_*f^*T_{F_n})^\vee$ and the morphism with $\phi_{F_n}$, since both are
obtained by differentiating the same universal evaluation map subject to the
relation $s\circ f=0$.
These maps and their commutativity
are preserved on overlaps, since they are induced by the universal
evaluation map and $ds$, rather than chosen quasi-isomorphisms.

In particular there is a morphism of distinguished triangles
\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
 j^*\mathbb E_{Y_n}&\longrightarrow&\mathbb E_{F_n}&\longrightarrow&(j^*E_+)^\vee[1]\\
 \downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
 j^*\mathbb L_{M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}/\mathfrak B}&\longrightarrow&
 \mathbb L_{M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}/\mathfrak B}&\longrightarrow&
 \mathbb L_{M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}/M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}}.
\end{array}
\]
This is the compatibility required in
\cite[Definition 4.5]{Manolache}; it is stronger than an equality of
classes in $K$-theory. The relative theory for $j$ is concentrated in
degree $-1$, namely $(j^*E_+)^\vee[1]$.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{3. The virtual cycle and its pushforward.}
The morphisms to $\mathfrak B$ and the closed immersion $j$ are of
Deligne--Mumford type. The stable-map stacks are proper finite-type
Deligne--Mumford stacks over $\mathbb C$ and satisfy the quotient-stratification
hypothesis by \cite[Remark 3.2]{Manolache}. The three relative theories
above are perfect of amplitude $[-1,0]$. Thus
\cite[Corollary 4.9]{Manolache}, with the compatible triple
just constructed, applies and gives
\[
 [M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}]^{\mathrm{vir}}=j^!_{E_+}[M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}]^{\mathrm{vir}}.
\]
The virtual pullback is the one defined by the normal-cone embedding
$C_{M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}/M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}}\hookrightarrow j^*E_+$ associated with
the section $\sigma$. In particular it is the refined pullback of the
zero section of $E_+$ in the Cartesian zero-locus square. For this
pullback the pushforward identity is
\[
 j_*j^!_{E_+}(\alpha)=c_{m+1}(E_+)\cap\alpha.
\]
One can see the identity by deforming the graph of $\sigma$ to the zero
section through the graphs of $t\sigma$, or by zero-section
self-intersection and compatibility of refined pullback with proper
pushforward. No regularity of $j$ is used. In the present smooth ambient
case the same formula is
$[M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}]^{\mathrm{vir}}=0^!_{j^*E_+}[C_{M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}/M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}}]$;
this is precisely the zero-section construction of \cite[Section 5]{BF}.
This proves $j_*[M_{F_n}^{(\ell)}]^{\mathrm{vir}}=e(E_+)[M_{Y_n}^{(\ell)}]^{\mathrm{vir}}$.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{4. The negative twist and marked evaluation.}
The universal curves are Cartesian under $j$, and
$i^*\mathcal O_{Y_n}(-H)=K_{F_n}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:basechange} therefore gives the
canonical identification $j^*E_-=R^1\pi_*f^*K_{F_n}=\mathcal V$.
It respects the fiber character of weight $\lambda$. Multiplication by
$e_\lambda(E_-)$ and the projection formula prove~\eqref{eq:pushvirtual}, including its assertion for arbitrary $\ell$.
The cotangent lines and evaluations pull back under $j$, since the
universal marked curve is unchanged. The same comparison consequently
holds with any product of descendants and insertions pulled back from $Y_n$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:virtual} identifies the resulting invariants with those
of $X_n$.

For $\ell=1$, evaluation of $f^*\mathcal O_{Y_n}(H)$ at the marking is
surjective on every fiber and hence over the whole stack. Thus
$0\to E'_+\to E_+\to\operatorname{ev}_{Y_n}^*\mathcal O_{Y_n}(H)\to0$ is an exact sequence
of vector bundles. It implies
$e(E_+)=\operatorname{ev}_{Y_n}^*H\,e(E'_+)$. Push forward~\eqref{eq:pushvirtual}, multiplied
by $\psi^a$, along evaluation, and use
$\operatorname{ev}_{Y_n}\circ j=i\circ\operatorname{ev}_{F_n}$. This proves~\eqref{eq:pushC}.
Finally pairing with $b$ and using
$\int_{Y_n} H b u=\int_{F_n} i^*(bu)$ proves~\eqref{eq:ambientpair}.
Only this numerical pairing is asserted in general; no injectivity of
$i_*$ on the full cohomology of $F_n$ has been used.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:CCITtoric}
Let $\boldsymbol\Sigma=(N,\Sigma,\rho)$ be a stacky fan defining a smooth
toric Deligne--Mumford stack $\mathcal X$ with projective coarse moduli
space, and let $S$ be a finite set with a map to $N_\Sigma$. Then the
$S$-extended nonequivariant $I$-function is a $\Lambda_{\rm nov}[[x,t]]$-valued
point of the nonequivariant genus-zero Givental cone of $\mathcal X$, at
$-z$ in the cone convention.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:CCITqrr}
The operator
\[
 \Delta=\prod_{j=1}^r\exp\left(
 \sum_{a,b\geq0}s_{a+b-1}\frac{B_b(0)}{b!}\frac{\rho_j^a}{a!}z^{b-1}\right)
\]
is a symplectic isomorphism from the untwisted to the $c$-twisted loop
space, and $\mathcal L^{c,B}=\Delta\,\mathcal L^{\rm un}$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:CCIThyper}
The family $\tau\mapsto I^{c,B}(\tau,-z)$ is a point of $\mathcal L^{c,B}$
over $\Lambda[[s_0,s_1,\ldots]][[\tau]]$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:CCITcone}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=*]
\item If $I(t)\in\mathcal L^{\rm tw}(R[[t]])$ then
 $I'(t)\in T_{I(t)}\mathcal L^{\rm tw}(R[[t]])$.
\item For the untwisted cone, $f\in\mathcal L(R)$ and $x\in R_{\rm nilp}$
 imply $(1+x)f\in\mathcal L(R)$.
\item $T_f\mathcal L(R)$ is an $R\{z\}$-submodule of the ambient tangent space.
\item If $I(t)\in\mathcal L(R[[t]])$ and $\xi(t)$ is tangent at $I(t)$, then
 $z\xi'(t)$ is tangent at $I(t)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:mirror}
The series $-zI^{\mu,\lambda}(\mathbf x,-z)$ lies on the mixed-twisted
Givental cone. In the convention $J=z\mathbf1+\tau+O(z^{-1})$,
\[
 zI^{\mu,\lambda}=J_{Y_n}^{\mu,\lambda}(\tau,z).
\]
Here Novikov and divisor variables are combined by the divisor equation,
as specified in the proof. Consequently the normalized zero-input series is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Bdef}
 B^{\mu,\lambda}=e^{-\sum_{i=1}^n  p_i\log Q_i/z}e^{\lambda g/z}
 I^{\mu,\lambda}
 =1+(\lambda-H)\sum_{\beta>0,a\geq0}
 \mathbf Q^\beta z^{-a-2}\mathsf E_{a,\beta}^{\mu,\lambda}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
We separate the toric input, the formal product modification, and the
specialization and normalization steps.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{1. Toric input, variables, and formal topology.}
The ambient variety $Y_n=(\mathbb P^1)^n$ is smooth and projective. Its fan is
complete and nonsingular, its stabilizers are trivial, and its anticanonical
class is $2H$. Thus Theorem~\ref{thm:CCITtoric} applies with no extended
variables and with the ambient torus parameters set to zero. It puts the
untwisted toric series on the untwisted cone. Its positive-degree terms
have order at most $z^{-1}$ after multiplication by $z$, since their
denominators have $z$-degree $2D\geq2$. The unique cone section with
expansion $z\mathbf1+\sum_i p_it_i+O(z^{-1})$ is therefore the small
$J$-function, which is
\[
 J_{Y_n}(\mathbf t,z)=ze^{\sum_i p_it_i/z}
 \sum_{\mathbf d\geq0}\mathbf q^{\mathbf d}e^{\sum_i d_it_i}
             \prod_{i=1}^n\prod_{r=1}^{d_i}(p_i+rz)^{-2}.
\]
Here $\mathbf q$ denotes independent Novikov variables. The substitution
$x_i=q_ie^{t_i}$ is a relabeling of divisor-weighted Novikov monomials;
in this notation the customary divisor exponential is recorded using
formal logarithms of $x_i$. 
                                         
Equivalently all identities below can be kept in $(\mathbf q,\mathbf t)$
until the last step, so no evaluation of a Novikov series at $q_i=1$ is
required.

Use the full primary input $\mathbf t$ on $H^*(Y_n)$ during the cone
argument; its restriction to the displayed divisor coordinates will be
taken afterwards. We use the cone convention in which $J_{Y_n}(\mathbf t,-z)$
lies on $\mathcal L_{Y_n}$. Formal points and tangent vectors are those of
Section~\ref{sec:mirrorinputs}; positive powers of $z$ are permitted when
their coefficients tend to zero in the coefficient-ring topology.
Initially retain finitely many characteristic parameters and work modulo
a power of their maximal ideal and of the Novikov/input ideal. The
differential operators below are then finite-order operators at each
characteristic-parameter degree. All constructions are compatible with
these quotients and with enlarging the finite set of parameters. This
specifies the inverse-limit interpretation of the subsequent series.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{2. Two independent characteristic classes.}
Put $\rho_+=H$, $\rho_-=-H$, and $d_+=D$, $d_-=-D$, the cohomology
classes on $Y_n$.
                                                                  
 Introduce parameters
$s_{j,k}$ for $j\in\{+,-\}$ and $k\geq0$, and set
\[
 s_j(w)=\sum_{k\geq0}s_{j,k}\frac{w^k}{k!},\qquad
 G_j(w,z)=\sum_{a,b\geq0}s_{j,a+b-1}
            \frac{B_b(0)}{b!}\frac{w^a}{a!}z^{b-1},\qquad s_{j,-1}=0.
\]
The twist is
$\exp(\sum_{j,k}s_{j,k}\operatorname{ch}_k(R\pi_*f^*\mathcal B_j))$,
where $\mathcal B_\pm=\mathcal O_{Y_n}(\pm H)$. The genus-zero quantum Riemann--Roch formula of
Theorem~\ref{thm:CCITqrr} gives
\[
 \mathcal L_{s_+,s_-}=\Delta\mathcal L_{Y_n},
 \qquad \Delta=\exp G_+(\rho_+,z)\exp G_-(\rho_-,z).
\]
For independent classes, the exponents in the Riemann--Roch calculation
add up, since differentiating the twisting class with respect to
$s_{j,k}$ inserts the Chern character of the corresponding index bundle.
The Riemann--Roch expression for that insertion does not
change when the other twist is present. The two multiplication operators
commute. This proves the product form of $\Delta$. This fact alone does
not prove hypergeometric modification; that is the separate argument
in the next two steps.

The Bernoulli generating series gives
$G_j(w+z,z)-G_j(w,z)=s_j(w)$. Consequently the degree-$\mathbf d$
modification at $-z$ is
\[
 M_{\mathbf d}(-z)=
 \prod_{j=+,-}\exp\{G_j(\rho_j,z)-G_j(\rho_j-d_jz,z)\}.
\]
For positive $d_j$ this telescopes through $d_j$ terms; for negative
$d_j$ the same identity gives the inverse product with the complementary
endpoints. In particular the formula does not require either $\mathcal B_j$ to
be nef. The standard hypergeometric theorem with a single characteristic
class is Theorem~\ref{thm:CCIThyper}; we now supply its
independent-class extension explicitly.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{3. Reduction to differential operators on the untwisted cone.}
Let $\nabla_j$ be the constant primary direction $\rho_j$, so on the divisor
slice $\nabla_+=\sum_{i=1}^n\partial_{t_i}$ and $\nabla_-=-\nabla_+$.
The divisor equation, applied to the degree-$\mathbf d$ part of the full
$J$-family, reads
\[
 -z\nabla_j J_{Y_n,\mathbf d}(\mathbf t,-z)
     =(\rho_j-d_jz)J_{Y_n,\mathbf d}(\mathbf t,-z).
\]
The descendant term at the output marking supplies the cup-product
term $\rho_j$; all other inputs are primary. This also follows directly
on the divisor slice from $e^{-\sum p_it_i/z}e^{\sum d_it_i}$.
The sign here is fixed by using $J(\mathbf t,-z)$.
After applying $\Delta^{-1}$, the modified series is therefore
\[
 \mathfrak F_s=\exp\{-G_+(-z\nabla_+,z)-G_-(-z\nabla_-,z)\}
                         J_{Y_n}(\mathbf t,-z).
\]
All operators in this exponent commute. For each retained parameter,
\[
 \partial_{s_{j,k}}\mathfrak F_s=D_{j,k}\mathfrak F_s,\qquad
 D_{j,k}=-\sum_{b=0}^{k+1}
 \frac{B_b(0)}{b!(k+1-b)!}
               (-z\nabla_j)^{k+1-b}z^{b-1}.
\]
We will prove that $\mathfrak F_s$ is a point of the untwisted cone.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{4. Tangency and the complete induction.}
We use the four statements of Proposition~\ref{prop:CCITcone}:
item (i) for derivatives of cone-valued families; item (ii) for conical
scaling; item (iii) for multiplication of tangent vectors by nonnegative
powers of $z$; and item (iv) for the operation $\xi\mapsto z\partial_t\xi$
on a tangent family along a cone-valued family.
These statements hold over the formal coefficient rings specified above.
For a cone-valued family $f(\mathbf t)$, every term in $D_{j,k}f$
is tangent to the cone along $f$. The potentially negative power of
$z$ can be checked by setting $b=0$, in which case the operator reduces
to a scalar multiple of $\nabla_j(z\nabla_j)^k$.
Start with the tangent vector $\nabla_jf$ and
apply Corollary B.7 exactly $k$ times. If $b\geq1$ and
$a=k+1-b\geq1$, the operator is, up to sign,
$z^b(z\nabla_j)^{a-1}\nabla_j$; the same argument and Proposition B.3
apply. If $a=0$, it is a multiple of $z^k f$, which is tangent by
Propositions B.2 and B.3. Thus we never divide an arbitrary tangent
vector by $z$.

The induction is on ordinary total degree in a fixed finite
set of characteristic parameters, not on their indices. In the formal
polarization write the graph equations of $\mathcal L_{Y_n}$ as
$\mathscr E(f)=0$, meaning that the negative component is the differential
of the genus-zero descendant potential evaluated at the positive
component after the dilaton shift. At $s=0$ the equations hold.
Assume $\mathscr E(\mathfrak F_s)\in(s)^r$ for $r\geq1$.
Take $\widetilde{\mathfrak F}_s$ to be the graph point with the same
positive component as $\mathfrak F_s$. Then
$\mathfrak F_s-\widetilde{\mathfrak F}_s\in(s)^r$.
All $D_{j,k}$ differentiate only the primary input and hence preserve
$(s)^r$. The chain rule and the preceding tangency calculation give
\[
 \partial_{s_{j,k}}\mathscr E(\mathfrak F_s)
 =d\mathscr E_{\mathfrak F_s}(D_{j,k}\mathfrak F_s)
 =d\mathscr E_{\widetilde{\mathfrak F}_s}
       (D_{j,k}\widetilde{\mathfrak F}_s)+O((s)^r)
 =O((s)^r).
\]
Each homogeneous monomial of degree $r$ has a nonzero derivative of
degree $r-1$ with respect to some parameter. Characteristic zero now
implies that the homogeneous part of degree $r$ in every graph equation
vanishes. Thus $\mathscr E(\mathfrak F_s)\in(s)^{r+1}$, proving the
induction. It includes mixed monomials in the two parameter sets.
Passing to the compatible completions proves cone membership. Applying
$\Delta$ proves the two-class hypergeometric assertion and restricting
the full primary input to divisors gives the required family.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{5. Euler and inverse-Euler specialization.}
Specialize to $c_+(w)=\mu+w$ and $c_-(w)=(\lambda+w)^{-1}$:
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
 s_{+,0}=\log\mu,&
 s_{+,k}=(-1)^{k-1}(k-1)!\mu^{-k}&(k\geq1),\\
 s_{-,0}=-\log\lambda,&
 s_{-,k}=(-1)^k(k-1)!\lambda^{-k}&(k\geq1).
\end{array}
\]
The formal meaning is the equivariant characteristic-class specialization
described in \cite[Section 2.3]{CCITtwisted}. Its validity in this argument is justified as follows.
The rank contributions are first written as powers of $e^{s_{+,0}}$ and
$e^{s_{-,0}}$, then specialized to powers of $\mu$ and $\lambda^{-1}$.
The remaining operations are expansions in inverse weights. At fixed
curve degree and fixed insertions the non-equivariant Chern classes have
bounded degree on the proper moduli stack. Thus the resulting correlators
are rational functions of the weights; their expansions determine them
injectively. The same is true of each finite hypergeometric ratio.
The assertion is therefore a rational-function identity, not an analytic
substitution of logarithms into an arbitrary characteristic-parameter
power series. 
Equivalently, the cone graph equations can be specialized
coefficientwise. At fixed curve degree, the positive-degree
input has positive Novikov order, so only finitely many
such inputs contribute. Once the remaining input degree is
fixed, dimension bounds ensure that only finitely many
Chern and descendant operations are nonzero.
This justifies specializing the formal identity obtained in Step 4.

At $z$ the two finite ratios are
\[
 \frac{\prod_{r=-\infty}^{D}(\mu+H+rz)}
      {\prod_{r=-\infty}^{0}(\mu+H+rz)}
       =\prod_{r=1}^{D}(\mu+H+rz),
 \]
 \[
 \frac{\prod_{r=-\infty}^{-D}(\lambda-H+rz)^{-1}}
      {\prod_{r=-\infty}^{0}(\lambda-H+rz)^{-1}}
       =\prod_{r=0}^{D-1}(\lambda-H-rz).
\]
The infinite-product notation only cancels identical tails. The inverse
Euler twist of the negative line contributes the second numerator, since
its index bundle is $-E_-$ in positive degree. In degree zero that index
bundle is $\mathcal B_-$ instead, yielding the reciprocal in the pairing.
The two factors produce exactly~\eqref{eq:Imixed}, proving the asserted
cone membership over $\mathbb Q(\mu,\lambda)$.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{6. The normalized $J$-section and the evaluation series.}
For $D>0$ the numerator has $z$-degree $2D-1$, while the denominator has
degree $2D$. The factor at $r=0$ in the negative product is $\lambda-H$;
the leading coefficient of the summand is
\[
 \frac{(\lambda-H)(-1)^{D-1}D!(D-1)!}{z\prod_{i=1}^n(d_i!)^2}.
\]
It is independent of $\mu$. Consequently
$I^{\mu,\lambda}=1+\tau/z+O(z^{-2})$ with the $\tau$ in the statement.
Uniqueness of the graph section with positive part $z\mathbf1+\tau$
gives $zI^{\mu,\lambda}=J_{Y_n}^{\mu,\lambda}(\tau,z)$ in the positive-$z$
convention. The string equation, with the twist-compatible derivation in
Appendix~\ref{app:forget}, removes the unit input $-\lambda g$,
and the divisor equation removes the divisor exponential, giving the
first expression in~\eqref{eq:Bdef}.

To verify the second expression without taking a degenerate limit, define
the ordinary evaluation pushforward
\[
 \mathsf V_{a,\beta}^{\mu,\lambda}
  =(\operatorname{ev}_{Y_n})_*\bigl(\psi^a e_\mu(E_+)e_\lambda(E_-)
                                     [M_{Y_n}]^\mathrm{vir}\bigr).
\]
Setting $w=(\mu+H)/(\lambda-H)$, contraction with the inverse
twisted pairing yields $w^{-1}\mathsf V_{a,\beta}^{\mu,\lambda}$.
Indeed, pairing this class with any $b$ gives
$\int_{Y_n} b\mathsf V_{a,\beta}^{\mu,\lambda}$, as required.
By the marked exact sequence,
$\mathsf V_{a,\beta}^{\mu,\lambda}=(\mu+H)\mathsf E_{a,\beta}^{\mu,\lambda}$.
Thus $w^{-1}\mathsf V=(\lambda-H)\mathsf E$. Finally the expansion
$1/(z(z-\psi))=\sum_{a\geq0}\psi^a z^{-a-2}$ gives precisely~\eqref{eq:Bdef}. Every coefficient of $\mathsf E$ is polynomial in
$\mu,\lambda$, so this identity proves regularity at $\mu=0$ before
specialization. The comparison with $F_n$ then follows from
Proposition~\ref{prop:virtualcompare}; it initially gives a comparison against ambient
classes. Theorem~\ref{thm:fullambient} identifies the evaluation classes as
ambient, and nondegeneracy then gives equality of the full one-point cohomology classes,
including in even dimension.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
This is a theorem about a cohomological Givental cone, not a quantum-$K$
cone. The terminology ``quantized symplectic cone'' is not needed.
Equation~\eqref{eq:Bdef} proves regularity at $\mu=0$ before taking a
limit of a degenerate pairing. Combining it with
Proposition~\ref{prop:virtualcompare} proves the local comparison
\emph{against all ambient insertions}. The additional geometric
Theorem~\ref{thm:fullambient} proves ambientness of the full one-point
evaluation series also for odd $n$, and therefore upgrades this comparison
to the full one-point cohomology-valued series. Its proof does not use the mirror theorem.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:division}
The quotient $U^\lambda=(B^\lambda-1)/(\lambda-H)$ is uniquely defined
in this completed ring. For every ambient $b$,
\[
 \int_Fi^*b\,i^*U^\lambda
 =\sum_{\beta>0,a\geq0}\mathbf Q^\beta z^{-a-2}
                         \int_Fi^*b\,C_{a,\beta}^\lambda.
\]
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Substitution $\lambda=H$ annihilates every positive-degree term of
$I_{X_n}^{\lambda,\mathrm{amb}}$. The remaining exponentials cancel because
$\log Q_i=\log x_i+g$ and $\sum p_i=H$. Thus $B^H=1$.
The remainder theorem for the monic polynomial $\lambda-H$ applies
coefficientwise even though $H$ is nilpotent. Multiplication by this
monic polynomial is injective in each polynomial coefficient ring,
which also proves uniqueness after completion.
Equation~\eqref{eq:Bdef} identifies the quotient with the generating
series of $\mathsf E_{a,\beta}^{0,\lambda}$ on $Y_n$.
Use~\eqref{eq:ambientpair} term by term.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:extraction}
The mirror coordinate is invertible as a germ at zero. For every
$0\leq a\leq n-2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:extraction}
 {
 \mathcal D_a^\Delta(Q)=-\frac{n!}{(n-2-a)!}\,K_{a+2}(y(Q)).}
\end{equation}
These are convergent germs with rational coefficients, and the equality
holds without any assumption about primitive middle cohomology.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Each positive-degree term of the untwisted-in-$\lambda$ local numerator
contains $-H$. Its degree-zero part is zero, and its degree-one part
is $H(-1)^D\binom D{\mathbf d}^{2}/D$. This proves the formula for $R$
and the vanishing of the $z^{-1}$ term in~\eqref{eq:Kdef}.
Symmetry and homogeneity give~\eqref{eq:Kdef}, with $K_j(0)=0$.
Specializing $(\lambda-H)U^\lambda=B^\lambda-1$ at $\lambda=0$ gives
\[
 -HU^0=\sum_{j=2}^nH^jz^{-j}K_j.
\]
In $\mathcal R^{S_n}$ the kernel of multiplication by $H$ is $\mathbb Q H^n$.
Therefore
$U^0=-\sum_{j=2}^nH^{j-1}z^{-j}K_j$ modulo that kernel.
Its restriction to $F_n$ kills $H^n$, so pairing the quotient with
$\delta_a$ gives~\eqref{eq:extraction}, using $\int_FH^{n-1}=n!$.
Only the ambient pairing assertion of Lemma~\ref{lem:division} was used.

For convergence, $c_D\leq n^{2D}$ because the sum of multinomial
coefficients is $n^D$. 
At fixed cohomological degree, expanding the finite products and
their inverses introduces at most a fixed power of
$1+\log(D+1)$ into the bound, since their coefficients are
polynomials in harmonic sums of the form $\sum_{r\leq D}r^{-k}$.
The same applies to the local series and
its exponential normalization. Thus $g$ and every $K_j$ converge for
$|y|<n^{-2}$. Since $Q=y+O(y^2)$, the inverse-function theorem gives
$y(Q)$ and the convergent germs in~\eqref{eq:extraction}.
All operations used rational coefficients.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
For $a=n-2$ the required function is $K_n$. Its coefficient $H^nK_n$
is zero after restriction to $F_n$. Division before restriction recovers
$-H^{n-1}K_n$, which can be integrated on $F_n$.
Thus discarding the ambient top term before division loses a 
numerical descendant. No cancellation of a nilpotent class is being
performed on $F_n$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:serre}
Coefficientwise in the completed ambient ring,
\[
 z\theta_yI_{X_n}^{0,\mathrm{amb}}=H\mathcal I^{\sharp},\qquad
 A=\sum_{D\geq0}(-1)^Dc_Dy^D=\theta_yR.
\]
For $0\leq j\leq n-1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:vtriangular}
 v_j=\frac{R^j}{j!}
 +\sum_{k=2}^j\frac{R^{j-k}}{(j-k)!}K_k
 +\sum_{k=2}^{j+1}\frac{R^{j-k+1}}{(j-k+1)!}\theta_Q K_k,
\end{equation}
where $K_k$ is read as a function of $Q$, and empty sums are zero.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
In degree $D$, $z\theta_y$ multiplies by $H+Dz$.
For $D>0$,
\[
 \prod_{r=0}^{D-1}(-H-rz)=(-1)^DH\prod_{r=1}^{D-1}(H+rz).
\]
Multiplying by $H+Dz$ completes the second positive product, giving
$H$ times the degree-$D$ summand of~\eqref{eq:Isharp}. In degree zero
both sides are $He^{H\log y/z}$. This proves the first identity.
Its coefficient of $H$ gives $A=\theta_yR$, while the degree-zero
cohomology part of~\eqref{eq:Isharp} gives its displayed series.
Now differentiate~\eqref{eq:Kdef} at $z=1$ and use
$\theta_y=A\theta_Q$. Comparing the coefficient of $H^{j+1}$ for
$0\leq j\leq n-1$ gives~\eqref{eq:vtriangular}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:firstlog}
The first logarithmic period satisfies
\[
 \frac{W_1}{A}=R+\theta_Q K_2
 =R-\frac{(n-2)!}{n!}\theta_Q\mathcal D_0^\Delta.
\]
More explicitly, with $\mathfrak h_D=\sum_{r=1}^D1/r$ and $\mathfrak h_0=0$,
\[
 W_1=A\log y+
 \sum_{D\geq1}(-1)^Dy^D\sum_{|\mathbf d|=D}\binom D{\mathbf d}^2
 \left(2\mathfrak h_D-\frac2n\sum_i \mathfrak h_{d_i}\right).
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Take $j=1$ in~\eqref{eq:vtriangular} and use
Theorem~\ref{thm:extraction}. For the explicit expansion, differentiate
the finite products to first cohomological degree; their linear term
is $2\mathfrak h_DH-2\sum_i \mathfrak h_{d_i}p_i$. Summing over all degree tuples replaces
the summed expression involving the second sum by $\frac Hn\sum_i \mathfrak h_{d_i}$, by permutation symmetry.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:operator}
Set $T_0=1$, $T_1=\theta_y/n$, and recursively define
\[
 T_{k+1}=\frac{\theta_yT_k+k\,yT_{k-1}}{n-k}
 \quad(1\leq k<n),\qquad
 \mathscr S_n=n!\left(\theta_yT_n+n\,yT_{n-1}\right).
\]
Expand uniquely
\[
 \mathscr S_n=\sum_{j\geq0}y^jU_j(\theta_y),\qquad
 U_0(\theta_y)=\theta_y^{n+1}.
\]
Only finitely many $U_j$ are nonzero. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Palgorithm}
 {
 P_{n-1}(y,\theta_y)=\theta_y^{n-1}+
 \sum_{j\geq1}y^jU_j(\theta_y)
                     \prod_{r=1}^{j-1}(\theta_y+r)^2.}
\end{equation}
This is a finite construction over $\mathbb Q$, for each integer $n\geq4$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:PF}
The operator $P_{n-1}$ has order $n-1$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:PFcertificate}
 {
 P_{n-1}\mathcal I^{\sharp}(y,1)=H^{n-1} y^H=H^{n-1}+H^{n}\log y
 \quad\text{in }\mathcal R[[y]][\log y].}
\end{equation}
Its coefficient of $\theta_y^{n-1}$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:leadP}
 \prod_{0\leq j<n/2}\bigl(1+(n-2j)^2y\bigr).
\end{equation}
Thus it has no finite singular point on $y>0$.
The functions $W_0,\ldots,W_{n-2}$ form a local basis of homogeneous
solutions, $P_{n-1}W_{n-1}=1$, and $P_{n-1}W_n=\log y$.
Here $W_n$ is the ambient top coefficient already defined in
Section~\ref{sec:serre}; it must be retained before restriction to $F_n$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
We first explain $\mathscr S_n$. If $f_1,\ldots,f_n$ solve
$\theta_y^2f_i=-yf_i$ over a commutative coefficient algebra, let
$V_k$ be the average over all subsets of size $k$ of the product in
which those $k$ factors are replaced by $\theta_yf_i$.
The product rule gives
\[
 \theta_yV_k=(n-k)V_{k+1}-k\,yV_{k-1},\quad
 \theta_yV_0=nV_1,\quad\theta_yV_n=-n\,yV_{n-1}.
\]
Eliminating $V_1,\ldots,V_n$ yields
$\mathscr S_nV_0=0$, with exactly Definition~\ref{def:operator}.
Assign weights $1$ to $\theta_y$ and $2$ to $y$.
The commutator lowers weight, so induction gives
$\deg U_j\leq n+1-2j$ and $U_j=0$ for $2j>n+1$.
The leading coefficient of $\mathscr S_n$ is $1$.

Now work in the actual square-free algebra $\mathcal R$ and set
\[
 f_i(y)=\sum_{d\geq0}\frac{(-1)^dy^{d+p_i}}{\Gamma(d+1+p_i)^2}.
\]
Gamma functions of nilpotent variables mean their finite Taylor
expansions, and $y^{p_i}=1+p_i\log y$ with $y>0$, so no branch is chosen
anywhere. The recurrence of $\Gamma$ gives
\[
 (\theta_y^2+y)f_i=\frac{y^{p_i}}{\Gamma(p_i)^2}=0,
\]
because $\Gamma(w)^{-2}$ has a double zero at $w=0$ and $p_i^2=0$.
This is why the calculation uses the square-free algebra, not a
substitution $p_i=H/n$ that would destroy its relations.
Hence $h=\prod_if_i$ satisfies $\mathscr S_nh=0$.

On $y^{D+H}$ define $\Xi=\Gamma(\theta_y+1)^2$ by multiplication by
$\Gamma(D+H+1)^2$. Each multiplier is invertible.
Then
\[
 \Xi y^j\Xi^{-1}=y^j\prod_{r=1}^j(\theta_y+r)^2.
\]
Multiplication of $\Xi h$ by the constant invertible class
$\prod_i\Gamma(1+p_i)^2/\Gamma(1+H)^2$ yields exactly $\mathcal I^{\sharp}(y,1)$
of~\eqref{eq:Isharp}, alternating signs included.
It follows that
\[
 \left[\theta_y^{n+1}+
 \sum_{j\geq1}y^jU_j(\theta_y)\prod_{r=1}^j(\theta_y+r)^2\right]\mathcal I^{\sharp}=0.
\]
Since $\theta_y^2y^j=y^j(\theta_y+j)^2$, the operator in brackets is
$\theta_y^2P_{n-1}$, so $\theta_y^2P_{n-1}\mathcal I^{\sharp}=0$.

Write $P_{n-1}\mathcal I^{\sharp}=\sum_{D\geq0}y^{D+H}R_D$.
For $D>0$, $(D+H)^2R_D=0$ implies $R_D=0$ because $D+H$ is invertible.
For $D=0$, only the constant-degree part $\theta_y^{n-1}$ acts, giving
$R_0=H^{n-1}$. This proves~\eqref{eq:PFcertificate} including its
nonzero source; division by a nilpotent element has not occurred.
The degree bound for $U_j$ proves the order is at most $n-1$, and the
constant-degree coefficient proves it is exactly $n-1$.

For completeness, the highest weighted symbol of $\mathscr S_n$ is
the characteristic polynomial of the displayed $(n+1)$-dimensional
system with commuting variables. Over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-y})$ its eigenvalues
are $(n-2j)\sqrt{-y}$ for $0\leq j\leq n$ (the symmetric-power
representation of the two eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt{-y}$).
Pairing opposite eigenvalues, with an additional zero eigenvalue when
$n$ is even, shows that the highest coefficients of the $U_j$ are the
coefficients of the corresponding product of
$\theta_y^2+(n-2j)^2y$. The Gamma multiplication and division by
$\theta_y^2$ in~\eqref{eq:Palgorithm} convert this product to~\eqref{eq:leadP}.

Finally $W_j=(\log y)^j/j!+O(y(1+|\log y|)^j)$.
Comparing coefficients of $H^j$ in~\eqref{eq:PFcertificate} gives
$P_{n-1}W_j=0$ for $j<n-1$ and $P_{n-1}W_{n-1}=1$.
The different leading logarithmic powers prove linear independence
of the $n-1$ homogeneous solutions. They form a basis because the
operator has order $n-1$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{rem:unsigned}
      We use $y=-t$ throughout. This removes the alternating signs generated by
$t^j=(-1)^jy^j$ and avoids expressions such as $(-y)^H$, whose interpretation
would require a branch choice. The Euler operator is unchanged,
$t\partial_t=y\partial_y$.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:frobenius}
The origin is a regular singular point with indicial polynomial
$\rho^{n-1}$ and a single maximal unipotent logarithmic block.
For any constant $b$, all local solutions of $P_{n-1}f=b$ have the form
\[
 f=bW_{n-1}+\sum_{j=0}^{n-2}b_jW_j.
\]
Their boundary polynomial in $\log y$ determines the $b_j$ uniquely.
In particular a differential equation alone does not specify the
physical solution.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
The coefficient of $\theta^{n-1}$ is nonzero at zero, and all other
coefficient polynomials are holomorphic there; the Euler-operator
form gives regular singularity and the indicial polynomial.
Theorem~\ref{thm:PF} gives the logarithmic basis and a particular
solution. Continuation $\log y\mapsto\log y+2\pi i$ on this basis
has a single Jordan block, as is already seen on its leading
polynomials. The boundary normalization then determines each constant.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:operators} As an
      illustration we specialize to the cases of $n=4$ and $n=5$ in the symbolic
      implementation of the finite construction given in
      Appendix~\ref{app:code}.

\noindent
For $n=4$, the algorithm gives
\begin{equation}\label{e:P3}
 P_3=\theta_y^3+y(20\theta_y^3+30\theta_y^2+18\theta_y+4)
                   +64y^2(\theta_y+1)^3.
\end{equation}
For $n=5$, it gives
\begin{align}\label{e:P4}
P_4&=\theta_y^4+y Q_1(\theta_y)+y^2 Q_2(\theta_y)+y^3Q_3(\theta_y),\\      
 Q_1&=35\theta_y^4+70\theta_y^3+63\theta_y^2+28\theta_y+5,\cr
 Q_2&=259\theta_y^4+1036\theta_y^3+1580\theta_y^2+1088\theta_y+285,\cr
 \nonumber Q_3&=225\theta_y^4+1350\theta_y^3+2925\theta_y^2+2700\theta_y+900.
\end{align}
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:analyticdomain}
The Schwinger integral is absolutely convergent for $\Re s\leq n^2$
and holomorphic for $\Re s<n^2$. It is not absolutely convergent for
$\Re s>n^2$. Its analytic continuation to $\mathbb C\setminus[n^2,\infty)$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:simplex}
 I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}(s)=\int_{\Delta_n}\frac{\Omega}{\phi(u)-s}.
\end{equation}
For real $s<n^2$ it also equals
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Laplacepositive}
 \int_0^\infty e^{rs}\left(\int_{\Delta_n}e^{-r\phi(u)}\Omega\right)dr.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Set $x_i=t u_i$. Then $\prod dx_i/x_i=(dt/t)\Omega$ and
$W(x)=t/\phi(u)$. The radial integral gives
$\int_0^\infty e^{-t(1-s/\phi)}dt/\phi=1/(\phi-s)$.
Applied to the absolute value of the integrand, the same computation gives
$1/(\phi-\Re s)$ where $\Re s<\phi$ and $+\infty$ where $\Re s\geq\phi$.
By Tonelli's theorem, the Schwinger integral therefore converges absolutely
if and only if $\int_{\Delta_n}\Omega/(\phi-\Re s)$ is finite, and when it
does, Fubini's theorem allows the radial integration to be performed first,
which gives~\eqref{eq:simplex}.
Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\phi\geq n^2$, with equality only at
$u_i=1/n$. 
The required boundary integrability follows from the estimate
$\phi^{-1}\leq\min_i u_i$. On the sector
$u_1\leq\cdots\leq u_n$, we have $u_n\geq 1/n$, which
bounds the density by $n/(u_2\cdots u_{n-1})$.
Successively integrating
$0<u_1<\cdots<u_{n-1}<1$ is finite (each integration cancels the next
denominator). There are finitely many sectors.
For $\Re s<n^2$ the density is bounded by a constant times
$\Omega/\phi$, locally uniformly in $s$.
At $s=n^2$, the minimum of $\phi$ is nondegenerate on the simplex,
so the only new interior singularity is bounded by a constant times
$\|u-u_*\|^{-2}$ in real dimension $n-1$. It is integrable because
$n\geq4$. This endpoint is one of the essential uses of the standing hypothesis
$n\geq4$, alongside the integral curve-lattice identification.
For $\Re s>n^2$, an open set near $u_*$ gives radial
exponential growth, so absolute convergence fails.
For each compact subset of the slit plane,
$|\phi-s|^{-1}\leq C/\phi$, which proves holomorphic continuation
under the integral. Finally the integrand in~\eqref{eq:Laplacepositive} 
is nonnegative and its radial integral is~\eqref{eq:simplex}. Hence Tonelli's theorem permits us to interchange the radial and simplex integrals.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:sTaylor}
For $|s|<n^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sTaylor}
 I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}(s)=\sum_{m\geq0}a_m s^m,\qquad
 a_m=\int_{\Delta_n}\phi(u)^{-m-1}\,\Omega>0,
\end{equation}
and, as $m\to\infty$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sTaylorasympt}
 a_m={\pi^{n-1\over 2}\,n^{n/2-2-2m}\over m^{n-1\over 2}}\,\bigl(1+O(m^{-1})\bigr).
\end{equation}
Consequently the Taylor series of $I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}$ at $s=0$ has
radius of convergence exactly $n^2$, and it converges absolutely and
uniformly on $|s|\leq n^2$. For an integer $j\geq0$, the $j$th derivative
has a finite limit as $s\uparrow n^2$ along the real axis if and only if
$j<(n-3)/2$. In particular, for $n=4$ and $n=5$ the integral is continuous,
but not $C^1$, at the thresholds $s=16$ and $s=25$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Since $\phi\geq n^2>|s|$ on $\Delta_n$, the expansion
$(\phi-s)^{-1}=\sum_{m\geq0}s^m\phi^{-m-1}$ is dominated by
$(\phi-|s|)^{-1}\leq n^2(n^2-|s|)^{-1}\phi^{-1}$, and
$\int_{\Delta_n}\Omega/\phi=I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}(0)$ is finite by
Proposition~\ref{prop:analyticdomain}. Integrating~\eqref{eq:simplex} term by
term gives~\eqref{eq:sTaylor}.

For~\eqref{eq:sTaylorasympt}, write $u=u_*+v$ with $\sum_iv_i=0$ and use
$v'=(v_1,\ldots,v_{n-1})$ as coordinates. Since $\sum_iv_i=0$,
\[
 \phi(u_*+v)=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{n}{1+nv_i}=n^2+n^3\sum_{i=1}^nv_i^2+O(|v|^3),
 \qquad \sum_{i=1}^nv_i^2=v'^{\mathsf T}(I+J)\,v',
\]
where $J$ is the $(n-1)\times(n-1)$ matrix with all entries $1$, so that
$\det(I+J)=n$. The density of $\Omega$ at $u_*$ is $n^n$. By the
Cauchy--Schwarz argument in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:analyticdomain}, $u_*$ is the only point of
$\Delta_n$ at which $\phi=n^2$. Hence for every neighbourhood $N$ of $u_*$
there is $\delta>0$ with $\phi\geq n^2(1+\delta)$ on $\Delta_n\setminus N$,
and the contribution of $\Delta_n\setminus N$ to $a_m$ is at most
$(n^2(1+\delta))^{-m}I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}(0)$. On $N$ write
$\phi^{-m-1}=n^{-2m-2}\exp(-(m+1)\psi)$ with
$\psi=\log(\phi/n^2)=n\sum_iv_i^2+O(|v|^3)$. The multidimensional Laplace
method, for a smooth phase with a nondegenerate minimum and a smooth
amplitude, gives
\[
 a_m=n^{n-2m-2}\,\left(\frac{\pi}{nm}\right)^{n-1\over 2}\det(I+J)^{-1/2}
 \bigl(1+O(m^{-1})\bigr),
\]
which is~\eqref{eq:sTaylorasympt}. The root test now gives the radius $n^2$.
On $|s|\leq n^2$ the terms are bounded by $a_mn^{2m}$, which is of exact
order $m^{-(n-1)/2}$ and hence summable since $n\geq4$. For the $j$th
derivative, the terms $m(m-1)\cdots(m-j+1)a_ms^{m-j}$ are nonnegative and
nondecreasing in $s\in[0,n^2)$, so by monotone convergence the limit as
$s\uparrow n^2$ equals $\sum_m m(m-1)\cdots(m-j+1)a_mn^{2(m-j)}$, whose terms
are of exact order $m^{j-(n-1)/2}$. This is finite exactly when
$j<(n-3)/2$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:sTaylorcorrection}
The remainder in~\eqref{eq:sTaylorasympt} can be made explicit to the next
order:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sTaylorcorrection}
 a_m={\pi^{n-1\over 2}\,n^{n/2-2-2m}\over m^{n-1\over 2}}
 \left(1-\frac{3(n-1)}{8m}+O(m^{-2})\right).
\end{equation}
Unlike Proposition~\ref{prop:sTaylor}, the argument uses the Bessel
representation~\eqref{eq:Bessel} of Section~\ref{sec:checks}; this remark is
not used in any proof. Replacing $J_0(\sqrt T\,r)$ in~\eqref{eq:Bessel} by
$I_0(\sqrt s\,r)$ gives a function of $s$ that is holomorphic on $|s|<n^2$,
because $|I_0(\sqrt s\,r)|\leq e^{\sqrt{|s|}\,r}$ and
$K_0(r)^n=O(r^{-n/2}e^{-nr})$ as $r\to\infty$. Since $J_0(\mathrm iz)=I_0(z)$,
it agrees with $I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}$ for $s=-T\leq0$, and hence on the
whole disk. Expanding $I_0$ termwise gives
\[
 a_m=\frac{2^{n-1}}{4^m(m!)^2}\int_0^\infty r^{2m+1}K_0(r)^n\,dr .
\]
By~\cite[\S10.40]{ext:DLMF},
$K_0(r)^n=(\pi/(2r))^{n/2}e^{-nr}\bigl(1-n/(8r)+O(r^{-2})\bigr)$ uniformly for
$r\geq1$, and the integrals over $[0,1]$ are negligible compared with the
main term. Hence
\[
 \int_0^\infty r^{2m+1}K_0(r)^n\,dr=\Bigl(\frac\pi2\Bigr)^{n/2}
 \frac{\Gamma(2m+2-n/2)}{n^{2m+2-n/2}}
 \left(1-\frac{n^2}{8(2m+1-n/2)}+O(m^{-2})\right).
\]
Finally
$\binom{2m}m=4^m(\pi m)^{-1/2}\bigl(1-\frac1{8m}+O(m^{-2})\bigr)$ and
$\Gamma(2m+2-n/2)/\Gamma(2m+1)
=(2m)^{1-n/2}\bigl(1+\frac{(2-n)(4-n)}{16m}+O(m^{-2})\bigr)$. The leading
factors reproduce~\eqref{eq:sTaylorasympt}, and the three first-order terms
add up to
\[
 \frac1{8m}\left(-1+\frac{(2-n)(4-n)}2-\frac{n^2}2\right)=-\frac{3(n-1)}{8m}.
\]
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:pseudothresholds}
By~\eqref{eq:leadP}, the operator of Theorem~\ref{thm:PF} is also singular at
the pseudothresholds $s=(n-2j)^2$, $1\leq j<n/2$, which lie inside the disk
of Proposition~\ref{prop:sTaylor}. 
These points are genuine singularities of the operator and have the
same local exponents as the threshold. For $n=4$, the local exponents
at both $y=-1/16$ and $y=-1/4$ are
$\{0,\frac12,1\}$. For $n=5$, the local exponents at
$y=-1/25$, $y=-1/9$, and $y=-1$ are
$\{0,1,1,2\}$.
Nevertheless, Proposition~\ref{prop:analyticdomain} shows that the physical
integral is holomorphic at the pseudothresholds. The vanishing there concerns
only its singular component, not the singularity of the operator itself.
The exponent $(n-3)/2$ in
Proposition~\ref{prop:sTaylor} is the familiar threshold exponent of
$n$-particle phase space in two dimensions. The disk of
Proposition~\ref{prop:sTaylor} lives in the physical variable $s$ and should
not be confused with the $Q$-Taylor disk of Theorem~\ref{thm:Qradius}.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{input:Gamma}
For this smooth Fano hypersurface, the positive oscillatory integral is
\[
 \int_{\Delta_n}e^{-r\phi(u)}\Omega
 =\int_{F_n} I_{F_n}(r\mathbf1,-1)\,\widehat\Gamma_{F_n}\qquad(r>0).
\]
This is the specialization to $q_1=\cdots=q_n=r$ of
\cite[Section 2, equation (10)]{Iritani}, which states, for a smooth Fano
$F_n\subset(\mathbb P^1)^{n}$ of degree $(1,\ldots,1)$ and $q_1,\ldots,q_{n}>0$,
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R_{+}^{n-1}}e^{-\phi_q(w)}\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{dw_i}{w_i}
                   =\int_{F_n} I_{F_n}(q,-1)\widehat\Gamma_{F_n},
\]
\[
 \phi_q(w)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}q_iw_i+q_n\right)
           \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}w_i^{-1}+1\right),
\]
with ordinary cohomological Chern roots in the Gamma class. We use this identity
only as an analytic input. More precisely, equation~(10) of~\cite{Iritani} gives
the positive-real oscillatory integral in the $(n-1)$ independent variables
$w_i$, paired with the $\widehat\Gamma$-class of the degree-$(1,\ldots,1)$ Fano
hypersurface. Specializing $q_1=\cdots=q_n=r$ and making the change of variables
$$
u_i=\frac{w_i}{1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}w_j},
\qquad
u_n=\frac{1}{1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}w_j},
$$
identifies its positive-real integral with
$$
\int_{\Delta_n}e^{-r\phi(u)}\Omega .
$$
Thus the only external analytic identity used here is the corresponding
positive-real $\widehat\Gamma$-pairing. The passage from this identity to the
physical Schwinger integral is not quoted from~\cite{Iritani}: it is the
Laplace-transform argument of Theorem~\ref{thm:laplace}, including the factor
$(-1)^D$ derived in~\eqref{eq:laplace-degree-sign}.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:Gamma}
On $F_n$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Gammapoly}
 \widehat\Gamma_{F_n}\Gamma(1-H)=\widehat\Gamma_{X_n}|_{F_n}
 =\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\gamma_kH^k,
 \qquad
 \sum_{k\geq0}\gamma_kt^k
 =\exp\left(\sum_{r\geq1}\frac{2\zeta(2r+1)}{2r+1}t^{2r+1}\right).
\end{equation}
Thus $\gamma_0=1$, $\gamma_1=\gamma_2=0$,
$\gamma_3=2\zeta(3)/3$, $\gamma_5=2\zeta(5)/5$,
and $\gamma_6=2\zeta(3)^2/9$.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The tangent $K$-class is
$[T_{X_n}|_{F_n}]=[T_{Y_n}|_{F_n}]-[\mathcal O(H)]+[\mathcal O(-H)]$.
Therefore the Gamma class equals
$\prod_i\Gamma(1+2p_i)\,\Gamma(1-H)/\Gamma(1+H)$.
In the Taylor expansion
$\log\Gamma(1+w)=-\gamma_Ew+\sum_{k\geq2}(-1)^k\zeta(k)w^k/k$,
the factor $p_i^2=0$ makes the first logarithm sum to $-2\gamma_EH$.
The Gamma ratio cancels this linear term and all even powers,
leaving $\sum_{r\geq1}2\zeta(2r+1)H^{2r+1}/(2r+1)$.
Truncate above degree $n-1$ and exponentiate. This also explains why
products of odd zeta values first occur when $n\geq7$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:laplace}
Let $s=-T<0$ and $y=T^{-1}=-1/s>0$, with the real logarithm.
For $T$ sufficiently large (in particular for $T>n^2$),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:physicalGamma}
      {
 I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}(-1/y)=y\int_{F_n}\epsilon\bigl(\mathcal I^{\sharp}(y,1)\bigr)
                           \widehat\Gamma_{X_n}|_{F_n}.}
\end{equation}
It is an identity of convergent logarithmic germs. In particular
\begin{equation}\label{eq:physicalPF}
 P_{n-1}\left(\frac{I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}(-1/y)}{y}\right)=(-1)^{n-1} n!.
\end{equation}
Its leading boundary polynomial is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:boundary}
 I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}(-1/y)=n!y\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}
 \frac{(-1)^{n-1-k}\gamma_k}{(n-1-k)!}(\log y)^{n-1-k}
 +O\bigl(y^2(1+|\log y|)^{n-1}\bigr).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Insert Theorem~\ref{input:Gamma} into~\eqref{eq:Laplacepositive}.
The degree-$D$ coefficient has $r^{D-H}$, so its Laplace integral is
\[
 \int_0^\infty e^{-Tr}r^{D-H}dr
 =T^{-1-D+H}\Gamma(1+D-H).
\]
This identity for a nilpotent $H$ means finitely many derivatives of
the elementary Gamma integral. The key identity is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:laplace-degree-sign}
 \Gamma(1+D-H)=(-1)^D\Gamma(1-H)\prod_{k=1}^D(H-k).
\end{equation}
Multiplying the existing Fano numerator $\prod(H-k)$ gives the square
and the factor $(-1)^D$. Thus the result is
\[
 y\int_{F_n} y^{-H}\sum_{\mathbf d\geq0}(-1)^Dy^D
 \frac{\prod_{k=1}^D(H-k)^2}{\prod_i\prod_{k=1}^{d_i}(p_i-k)^2}
 \widehat\Gamma_{F_n}\Gamma(1-H),
\]
which is precisely~\eqref{eq:physicalGamma}.

To justify termwise integration, expand only to the finitely many
cohomological degrees that can contribute. The Fano scalar coefficients
are $D!/\prod d_i!^2$; integrating $r^D$ multiplies by
$D!T^{-D-1}$. Logarithmic derivatives introduce only fixed powers of
$1+\log(D+1)+|\log T|$; the same holds for finite product expansions.
The sum of the resulting absolute integrals is bounded by a constant
times $T^{-1}\sum_D(n^2/T)^D$ times such a fixed logarithmic power.
It converges for $T>n^2$, giving the required interchange.

Apply $P_{n-1}$ to~\eqref{eq:physicalGamma} and use
Theorem~\ref{thm:PF}. On $F_n$, the top-degree term is
$\epsilon(H^{n-1} y^H)=(-1)^{n-1}H^{n-1}$; the Gamma factor contributes only its
constant term. This gives~\eqref{eq:physicalPF}.
For~\eqref{eq:boundary} retain the degree-zero Novikov term
$y^{-H}$; all other terms satisfy the stated convergent-germ bound.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
\label{rem:analytic-source-sign}
Three separate conventions must be matched before any displayed formula is
transcribed between the present work and the one of Iritani~\cite{Iritani}.

First, the denominator in~\eqref{eq:simplex} is $\phi-s$, whereas the
amplitude in~\cite{Iritani} uses $s-\phi$; this is an overall sign,
independent of the curve degree. Second, the period normalizations
$\Pi_{n-1}=(-1)^{n-1}yA$ and $\pi=-yA$ differ with loop parity, as detailed in
Section~\ref{sec:dictionary}. Third, and least visible, is the degree
factor itself.
The degree factor can be incorporated in either of two equivalent ways.
Here it appears explicitly in the series~\eqref{eq:Isharp}, which contains
$(-1)^D$, with $y>0$ and the real logarithm understood.
Alternatively one may evaluate an unsigned
squared-numerator series at a negative argument, since
$(-x)^{\mathbf d}=(-1)^{D}x^{\mathbf d}$ when $|\mathbf d|=D$; this
produces the same factor automatically, but then leaves the branch of
$x^H$ at negative $x$ to be fixed (or its cohomological phase to be
removed separately). 
The displayed formula in Iritani's Theorem~8 therefore does not exhibit an additional
explicit $(-1)^D$ in that convention. 
 In the convention of the present paper the termwise Laplace transform of equation~(10) produces the factor $(-1)^D$ in~\eqref{eq:laplace-degree-sign};
this is the convention used in Theorem~\ref{thm:laplace} and in the subsequent numerical checks.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:assembly}
As convergent logarithmic germs at $s=-\infty$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:allloop}
      {
 I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}(s)=\Pi_{n-1}(s)\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k\gamma_k
              \mathcal T_{n-1-k}(R(s),Q(s)).}
\end{equation}
Its zeta-free bracket is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rationalbracket}
 \mathcal T_{n-1}=n\,R^{n-1}+\sum_{j=0}^{n-2}h_j(Q)R^j,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hj}
 h_{n-2}=-\theta_Q\mathcal D_0^\Delta,\qquad
 h_j=-(j+1)\mathcal D_{n-3-j}^\Delta
                 -\theta_Q\mathcal D_{n-2-j}^\Delta\quad(0\leq j\leq n-3).
\end{equation}
Here $\theta_Q=Q\partial_Q$ and ``zeta-free'' denotes the $k=0$ contribution in
the explicit Gamma expansion, and does not assume any unproved algebraic
independence of zeta values. Each $h_j$ has rational Taylor coefficients and
zero constant term.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The involution in~\eqref{eq:physicalGamma} acts by $(-1)^j$ on $H^j$.
Top-degree extraction therefore gives
\[
 I_{\circleddash}^{(n-1)}(s)=n!yA\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^{n-1-k}\gamma_kv_{n-1-k}
       =\Pi_{n-1}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k\gamma_k(n!v_{n-1-k}).
\]
Substitute~\eqref{eq:extraction} into~\eqref{eq:vtriangular}.
The resulting expression for $n!v_j$ is exactly~\eqref{eq:Vj}.
For $j=n-1$ the first coefficient is $n!/(n-1)!=n$; the two factorial
ratios simplify respectively to $n-2-a$ and $1$, giving~\eqref{eq:hj}.
Rationality and convergence follow from
Theorem~\ref{thm:extraction}. All signs and the factor of the curve
degree in $\theta_Q$ are retained.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:nfour}
For $n=4$ put $\Pi_3=-yA$ and
$\delta_0=H^2/2$. Then
\[
 I_3=\Pi_3\bigl[4R^3+f_2R^2+f_1R+f_0-16\zeta(3)\bigr],
\]
with
\[
 f_2=-\theta_Q\mathcal D_0^\Delta,\qquad
 f_1=-2\mathcal D_0^\Delta-\theta_Q\mathcal D_1^\Delta,\qquad
 f_0=-\mathcal D_1^\Delta-\theta_Q\mathcal D_2^\Delta,
\]
and
$\mathcal D_0^\Delta=-12K_2$, $\mathcal D_1^\Delta=-24K_3$,
$\mathcal D_2^\Delta=-24K_4$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Use $n!=24$, $\gamma_3=2\zeta(3)/3$ and
$\mathcal T_0=24$ in~\eqref{eq:allloop}; then apply~\eqref{eq:hj} and~\eqref{eq:extraction}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:nfive}
For $n=5$ put $\Pi_4=yA$. Then
\[
 I_4=\Pi_4\left[5R^4+\sum_{j=0}^3h_jR^j
      -80\zeta(3)\left(R-\frac1{20}\theta_Q\mathcal D_0^\Delta\right)\right],
\]
where
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 h_3=-\theta_Q\mathcal D_0^\Delta,&
 h_2=-3\mathcal D_0^\Delta-\theta_Q\mathcal D_1^\Delta,\\
 h_1=-2\mathcal D_1^\Delta-\theta_Q\mathcal D_2^\Delta,&
 h_0=-\mathcal D_2^\Delta-\theta_Q\mathcal D_3^\Delta,
\end{array}
\]
and $(\mathcal D_0^\Delta,\mathcal D_1^\Delta,\mathcal D_2^\Delta,\mathcal D_3^\Delta)
=(-20K_2,-60K_3,-120K_4,-120K_5)$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Now $n!=120$ and
$\mathcal T_1=120R-6\theta_Q\mathcal D_0^\Delta$.
Only $k=0,3$ contribute in~\eqref{eq:allloop}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:lowloop}
Corollaries~\ref{cor:nfour} and~\ref{cor:nfive} are the statements used in the
companion paper~\cite{PaperII}, that gives an independent analytic normalization
and a separate primary coefficient bridge for the $n=4$ identity from the
Picard--Fuchs equation and a Mellin transform, an explicit quantum-$K$ formula
and fourfold integrality statement at $n=4$, the numerical descendant
potentials, and the comparison of the $n=3,4,5$ normalizations with the
local--relative Euler factors.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
At $n=6$ the $\zeta(5)$ term first appears, in addition to the
$\zeta(3)$ term multiplying $\mathcal T_2$.
At $n=7$ the product $\zeta(3)^2$ appears.
Thus it would be incorrect to extrapolate the special $n=4,5$
pattern to a claim that only a single $\zeta(3)$ boundary term occurs
for every loop number. Formula~\eqref{eq:allloop} fixes both the zeta
polynomial and the descendant correction multiplying each of its terms.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:torus}
The power series in~\eqref{eq:mirrorcoordinate} extend to
$\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,-n^{-2}]$ by
\[
 A(y)=\int\frac{d\nu}{1+y\mathfrak q(\mathbf w)},\qquad
 g(y)=-\int\log(1+y\mathfrak q(\mathbf w))\,d\nu,
\]
using the principal logarithm. Their Taylor radii at zero are exactly
$n^{-2}$. For $y>0$, $A(y)>0$ and $Q(y)=ye^{g(y)}$ is strictly increasing.
It maps $(0,\infty)$ bijectively onto $(0,Q_\infty)$, where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qinfty}
 Q_\infty=\exp\left(-\int\log|w_1+\cdots+w_n|^2d\nu\right),
 \qquad n^{-2}\leq Q_\infty\leq1.
\end{equation}
The inverse $y(Q)$ is real analytic on that open interval.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
The constant term of
$(w_1+\cdots+w_n)^D(w_1^{-1}+\cdots+w_n^{-1})^D$
is $c_D$, so $c_D=\int \mathfrak q^D d\nu$. Summing the geometric and
logarithmic series for $|y|<n^{-2}$ gives the formulas.
On compact subsets of $\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,-n^{-2}]$ their denominators and logarithm
branches are uniformly controlled for $0\leq \mathfrak q\leq n^2$; hence they
are holomorphic there.
If $M_D=\binom{D+n-1}{n-1}$ is the number of compositions, then
Cauchy--Schwarz and the multinomial theorem give
\[
 \frac{n^{2D}}{M_D}\leq c_D\leq n^{2D}.
\]
Thus $\lim c_D^{1/D}=n^2$, proving the exact radii for $A$ and $g$.
For positive $y$, $yQ'(y)/Q(y)=1+yg'(y)=A(y)>0$.
Also
\[
 \log Q(y)=-\int\log(\mathfrak q(\mathbf w)+y^{-1})d\nu.
\]
The limiting logarithmic integral is finite. Indeed, conditioning on
$w_1,\ldots,w_{n-1}$ and writing $b=\sum_{i<n}w_i$, the elementary
one-variable Jensen formula gives
$\int_{S^1}\log|b+w_n|^2d\nu_n=2\log\max(1,|b|)$.
It is between $0$ and $2\log(n-1)$. For completeness, the circle identity follows by expanding
$\log(1+w/b)$ when $|b|>1$, and $\log(1+b/w)$ when $|b|<1$;
all nonconstant Fourier coefficients have mean zero. At $|b|=1$ the
remaining singularity is $2\log|2\sin(t/2)|$, which is integrable,
and gives the same limit. The positive part is bounded uniformly by
$2\log n$. Since the circle mean is nonnegative, the mean of the
negative part is also at most $2\log n$, uniformly for $|b|\leq n-1$.
Tonelli's theorem, applied to the two nonnegative parts, now proves absolute
integrability on the full torus. Fubini's theorem then computes
$\int\log\mathfrak q\,d\nu$ by first taking the circle mean in $w_n$ and
then integrating over $w_1,\ldots,w_{n-1}$; since that circle mean is
nonnegative, so is the integral. Monotone convergence applied after
subtracting an upper bound to $\log(\mathfrak q+y^{-1})$ proves the limit.
Since also $\mathfrak q\leq n^2$, the integral of $\log\mathfrak q$ lies
between $0$ and $2\log n$. This proves~\eqref{eq:Qinfty} and the
endpoint behavior. Strict monotonicity and the real inverse-function
theorem complete the proof.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:realcontinuation}
The germs $\mathcal D_a^\Delta$ admit a specified real analytic continuation
along $0<Q<Q_\infty$. Using these continued functions,~\eqref{eq:allloop} holds for every real $s<0$.
This assertion does not say that the original Taylor series in $Q$
converges on the entire interval.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The leading coefficient~\eqref{eq:leadP} never vanishes for $y>0$.
Thus all the $W_j$ used in Theorem~\ref{thm:serre} continue along the
positive real axis as solutions of their homogeneous or inhomogeneous
ordinary differential equations. Write
$I_{X_n}^{0,\mathrm{amb}}(y,1)=\sum_{j=0}^nH^jJ_j(y)$.
The identity $\theta_yI_{X_n}^{0,\mathrm{amb}}=H\mathcal I^{\sharp}$ says
$\theta_yJ_{j+1}=W_j$ for $0\leq j\leq n-1$.
It therefore continues the $J_j$ by integration, and hence the $K_j$
